blocks.text: The presynaptic neuron synthesises, transports and stores the chemical messenger (neurotransmitter). Synthesis takes place in the cell body/soma, which holds the protein-synthesis machinery; axonal transport then carries the neurotransmitter to the synaptic terminal, where it is stored in the synaptic vesicle until release by membrane fusion and exocytosis.

Released neurotransmitter occupies receptors on the postsynaptic membrane; some also acts on autoreceptors in the presynaptic membrane, which are crucial for feedback inhibition of neurotransmitter synthesis and release.

Neurotransmitters show specificity in receptor interaction (lock and key): one neurotransmitter can have more than one receptor type, but a given receptor site accepts only a particular chemical conformation. Receptors are finite in number and become saturated if neurotransmitter is over-secreted.

Receptor binding is often competitive - the relative synaptic concentrations of competing molecules decide the degree of receptor activity. Most receptors bind reversibly (the receptor returns to its physiological status quo after dissociation); some molecules act irreversibly, structurally altering the protein of the receptor complex.

blocks.title: How neurotransmitter action ends
rows: Reuptake back into the presynaptic neuron via special transporters
Removed by glia or plasma circulation

blocks.title: Points of feedback control of a neurotransmitter
rows: Independent postsynaptic inhibition via a different neuronal network

blocks.text: **Q15** asks which listed neurotransmitter is an amino acid: glycine is the answer (the others - acetylcholine, neurotensin, dopamine, endorphins - are not), and the explanation notes glycine acts both as a glutamate co-transmitter and as an independent inhibitory neurotransmitter at its own receptors.

blocks.note: Notes list histamine as a monoamine but give no precursor. **Q1** (serotonin-histidine is the wrongly matched pair) explains serotonin comes from tryptophan, and histamine is produced from histidine - not covered in the notes.

bullets.text: Presynaptic neuron synthesises (soma), transports (axonal transport) and stores (vesicle) the transmitter; release is by membrane fusion/exocytosis.
Autoreceptors on the presynaptic membrane give feedback inhibition of synthesis and release.
Receptor binding is lock-and-key, saturable, often competitive and mostly reversible (some molecules act irreversibly).
Action ends by reuptake via transporters, enzymatic breakdown at the cleft (COMT/MAO-A), or removal by glia/plasma (glutamate shuttle).
Five feedback-control points: synthesis, release, reuptake, autoreceptor presynaptic inhibition, independent postsynaptic inhibition via another network.
Classes: monoamines (DA, NE, epinephrine, 5HT, ACh, histamine); amino acids (GABA, glycine, glutamate); peptides (endorphins, CCK, neurotensin, NPY, leptin, ghrelin).

blocks.text: Receptors fall into three categories: ligand-gated channels (ionotropic), receptors coupled to intracellular G proteins as transducers (metabotropic), and ligand-dependent regulators of nuclear transcription (nuclear receptors).

blocks.title: Ionotropic vs metabotropic receptors
rows: Four or five protein subunits forming a pore ('doughnut with a hole'/'rosette'); **GABA-A** is the typical example
Proteins spanning the membrane seven times (serpentine receptors)
Inhibitory action: Cl- entry; excitatory action: Ca2+ or other cation entry
Cyclase-mediated second messenger activation (**GTP**, **ATP** etc.); Gs stimulatory, Gi inhibits adenylate cyclase; third variant acts via phospholipase C
Influence protein synthesis eventually, producing longer lasting effects
**DA** receptors, most 5HT receptors except 5HT3, norepinephrine and neuropeptide (incl. opioid) receptors

blocks.text: **GABA-A** receptor structure: each subunit is a string of amino acids passing in and out of the membrane four times; a large extracellular N-terminal is thought to mediate **GABA**-channel interactions, and a large intracellular loop in the middle has four phosphorylation sites.

Nuclear receptors (e.g. glucocorticoid receptors) belong to a superfamily with a cysteine-rich **DNA**-binding domain, a ligand-binding domain and a variable amino terminal region. On ligand binding the receptor becomes a transcription factor and binds **DNA** via zinc fingers. Others: progesterone, androgen and 1,25-dihydroxycholecalciferol (vitamin D) receptors; many are orphan receptors with unidentified ligands.

The glucocorticoid receptor sits mainly in the cytoplasm and migrates to the nucleus as soon as it binds its ligand; by contrast the estrogen and triiodothyronine (**T3**) receptors are retained in the nucleus and bind hormones there directly.

blocks.title: Receptor-class questions seen in the bank

items.text: Ionotropic = ligand-gated ion channel (**GABA-A** is pentameric ionotropic); 5-**HT3** is the ligand-gated cation channel among the 5-**HT** receptors; **GABA-B**, 5HT2A and **D2** are not ionotropic.
Glucocorticoid receptor = ligand-dependent regulator of nuclear transcription (translocates to nucleus to modulate gene expression), not ionotropic/metabotropic.
Beta receptors are Gs coupled and so increase adenylate cyclase; alpha1 is phospholipase C coupled and alpha2 is Gi coupled.
'Rosette shaped' was keyed to **NMDA** receptors in this bank; the explanation draws it from the **GABA-A** ionotropic structure (five subunits in a circle, each crossing the membrane four times).

bullets.text: Three receptor classes: ionotropic (ligand-gated channels), metabotropic (G-protein coupled), nuclear (ligand-dependent regulators of transcription).
Ionotropic = fast; metabotropic = slower but longer lasting (influences protein synthesis).
Ionotropic: GABA-A, NMDA, 5HT3; subunit pore ('rosette'); Cl- entry inhibitory, Ca2+/cations excitatory.
Metabotropic: seven-transmembrane; Gs stimulatory, Gi inhibits adenylate cyclase, third variant via phospholipase C; includes DA receptors and all 5HT except 5HT3.
Nuclear receptors become transcription factors after ligand binding and bind DNA via zinc fingers.
Glucocorticoid receptor: cytoplasmic, migrates to nucleus on binding; estrogen and T3 receptors are nuclear already.

blocks.title: Dopamine at a glance
rows: **MAO** and **COMT** (**MAO-A** more selective for norepinephrine and serotonin; **MAO-B** more selective for dopamine)
Motivation, novelty seeking, reward circuitry (addictions), arousal and motor movement gating in basal ganglia
Low in Parkinson's; high in psychosis (especially mesolimbic); may be low in anhedonia/negative symptoms (mesocortical)

blocks.title: Dopamine receptors
rows: **D1** exclusively postsynaptic, resistant to antagonism; **D5** more limbic, 10 times higher dopamine affinity
**D4** mainly frontal cortex, high **clozapine** affinity; **D4**-selective antagonists have no antipsychotic efficacy

blocks.text: All five dopamine receptors (**D1** to **D5**) are G-protein coupled.

blocks.title: Dopamine traps from the question bank

items.text: Rate-limiting step in dopamine synthesis is tyrosine hydroxylase (not dopamine beta hydroxylase, **PNMT**, **COMT** or choline acetyltransferase); **DOPA** is then converted to dopamine by **DOPA** decarboxylase.
Pairing 'dopamine - Alzheimer dementia' is the incorrect one: Alzheimer's is linked to acetylcholine deficiency (the pairings are over-simplifications).

**D2**-like receptors are inhibitory (negatively linked to adenylate cyclase); **D2** and **D3** can also sit presynaptically as autoreceptors - 'presynaptic inhibitory receptor' was the best description of **D2**.

blocks.note: **Q6** (hyperprolactinaemia on depot antipsychotic): tuberoinfundibular pathway (hypothalamus to anterior pituitary) normally tonically inhibits prolactin release. **Q32**: **D1** and **D2** predominate in caudate-putamen; **D3** nucleus accumbens, **D4** prefrontal cortex, **D5** hippocampus. Neither is in the notes (notes only name mesolimbic/mesocortical).
**Q10**: nicotinic stimulation (alpha-4-beta-2 subtype) regulates dopamine release in nucleus accumbens, a target of nicotine in tobacco. Not in the notes.

bullets.text: Tyrosine -> L-dopa -> dopamine; rate-limiting step tyrosine hydroxylase.
Broken down by MAO (MAO-B more selective for dopamine) and COMT to homovanillic acid; reuptake by the dopamine transporter (blocked by cocaine).
Functions: motivation, novelty seeking, reward (addiction), arousal, basal ganglia motor gating.
All five DA receptors are G-protein coupled: D1-like (D1, D5) stimulate adenylate cyclase; D2-like (D2, D3, D4) inhibit it.
D4 is frontal-cortical with high clozapine affinity, but D4-selective antagonists are not antipsychotic.
Low in Parkinson's; high mesolimbic in psychosis; possibly low mesocortical in negative symptoms/anhedonia.

blocks.title: Noradrenaline (norepinephrine) at a glance
rows: Dopamine-beta-hydroxylase modulates norepinephrine production; phenylethanolamine-N-methyltransferase modulates conversion to epinephrine
**MHPG** (major **CNS** metabolite) and **VMA** (vanillyl mandelic acid; major metabolite from peripheral nervous/endocrine system)
Arousal, anxiety, mood regulation, autonomic mediation
Low in depression; abnormal in panic/anxiety disorders

blocks.title: Adrenergic receptors
rows: Beta-1 high affinity for norepinephrine; beta-2 high affinity for epinephrine

blocks.text: Predominant **CNS** metabolite of noradrenaline is **MHPG** (3-methoxy-4-hydroxyphenylglycol); **VMA**, 5-**HIAA** and **COMT** were distractors.

blocks.subtopic: Locus coeruleus as noradrenergic cell-body site
blocks.note: **Q8**: principal **CNS** location of noradrenergic cell bodies is the locus coeruleus (pons/medulla clusters, with the lateral tegmental nuclei). The notes mention locus ceruleus only for beta-receptor predominance.
**Q16**: catecholamines are L-dopa, dopamine, norepinephrine and epinephrine (synthesised from tyrosine). The notes do not use the term.

bullets.text: Tyrosine -> L-dopa -> dopamine -> norepinephrine -> epinephrine; rate-limiting step tyrosine hydroxylase.
MAO (esp. MAO-A) and COMT break it down; MHPG is the major CNS metabolite, VMA the major peripheral/endocrine one.
Reuptake channel is inhibited by tricyclics and reboxetine.
Functions: arousal, anxiety, mood regulation, autonomic mediation; low in depression, abnormal in panic/anxiety.
Alpha-1 is phospholipase C coupled (postsynaptic); alpha-2 is Gi coupled (presynaptic autoreceptor); beta is Gs coupled.
Beta-1 has high affinity for norepinephrine; beta-2 for epinephrine.

blocks.title: Serotonin (5HT) at a glance
rows: Availability of tryptophan (so tryptophan depletion studies can manipulate the 5HT system)
Mood, perception of pain, feeding, sleep-wake cycle, motor activity, sexual behaviour, temperature regulation
Low serotonin -> increased depression, aggression, suicide, impulsivity; regulates dopamine system - role in psychosis

blocks.text: There are 14 known serotonin receptor subtypes (5-**HT1A**, 1B, 1D, 1E, 1F, 2A, 2B, 2C, 3, 4, 5A, 5B, 6, 7). All except 5-**HT3** are G-protein coupled; 5HT3 is predominant in gut and associated with motility.

blocks.title: Serotonin receptor coupling and location
rows: Antagonism -> antipsychotic response (atypicals) and sedation; **LSD** causes 5-**HT2** stimulation; down-regulated after antidepressant treatment/**ECT**
May be involved in antidepressant action

blocks.title: Serotonin receptor subtype and clinical action
rows: Antipsychotic (antagonist); hallucinogens (agonist/partial agonist); implicated in working memory; also in platelets and smooth muscles
Stimulation may produce cardiac valvular fibrosis (dexfenfluramine)

blocks.text: **DOPA** decarboxylase (**DDC**) is implicated in two pathways: after tyrosine hydroxylase makes L-**DOPA**, **DDC** decarboxylates it to dopamine (abundant in basal ganglia; precursor of noradrenaline and adrenaline in the adrenal medulla); in the nervous system tryptophan hydroxylase produces 5-**OH** tryptophan, which **DDC** decarboxylates to serotonin. **DDC** is a homodimeric, pyridoxal phosphate-dependent enzyme (**OMIM** excerpt).

Serotonin-histidine is the **INCORRECT** precursor pairing: serotonin comes from tryptophan (tryptophan hydroxylase then aromatic amino acid decarboxylase); histidine is the histamine precursor. Adrenaline-noradrenaline, dopamine-tyrosine, noradrenaline-dopamine and **GABA**-glutamate are correct.

blocks.note: **Q4**: serotonin is the most abundant transmitter in the median raphe nuclei; ascending projections from the raphe regulate mood, anxiety and sleep, descending projections may regulate pain. Not in the notes.
**Q33**: magic mushroom effects are very similar to **LSD** (psilocybin has a structure similar to **LSD** and is a prodrug for psilocin). The notes give no content on this.
**Q21**: khat (Catha edulis) has effects comparable to amphetamines (releases stimulants cathinone and cathine). Not in the notes.

bullets.text: Tryptophan -> 5-hydroxytryptophan -> serotonin; rate-limiting step is tryptophan availability (hence tryptophan depletion studies).
Broken down by MAO (preferentially MAO-A) to 5-HIAA; reuptake channel inhibited by tricyclics and SSRIs.
Functions: mood, pain, feeding, sleep-wake, motor activity, sexual behaviour, temperature.
14 receptor subtypes; all G-protein coupled except ionotropic 5-HT3 (gut, motility).
5HT1A agonist antidepressant, partial agonist anxiolytic; 5HT1B aggression; 5HT1D antimigraine antagonist.
5HT2A antagonism antipsychotic (atypicals) and sedating, agonism hallucinogenic (LSD); 5HT2B valvular fibrosis (dexfenfluramine); 5HT2C anxiogenic/anorexic; 5HT3 antagonist antiemetic.
Low serotonin: depression, aggression, suicide, impulsivity; modulates dopamine (psychosis).

blocks.title: Acetylcholine at a glance
rows: None; degraded choline is re-uptaken and recycled
Modulates arousal, learning, memory, **REM** sleep, pain perception, thirst and parasympathetic mediation
Reduced cholinergic function in Alzheimer's dementia; dopamine balance affected in Parkinson's

blocks.title: Cholinergic receptors
rows: G-protein coupled; five subtypes (**M1-M5**); more common than nicotinic in the **CNS**
Ion channels; more in peripheral parasympathetic system; less common than M receptors in **CNS**, where it mediates attention

blocks.text: Enzyme involved in acetylcholine synthesis is choline acetyltransferase (not acetylcholinesterase or butyrylcholinesterase, which degrade it).

Alzheimer's: cholinergic neurons fall, with reduced acetylcholinesterase and choline acetyltransferase (the rate-limiting synthetic enzyme) and reduced ACh; 'decreased levels of acetylcholinesterase' was the keyed answer, not increased ChAT or AChE.

blocks.subtopic: Nicotinic receptor pharmacology and cholinergic sites
blocks.note: **Q14**: tobacco nicotine stimulates nicotinic receptors (ligand-gated, rapid, excitatory, blocked by curare). Not in the notes.
**Q30** and **Q38**: most **CNS** cholinergic tracts originate in the nucleus basalis of Meynert (basal forebrain), projecting to cortex, hippocampus and amygdala. Not in the notes.

bullets.text: Made from choline and acetyl-CoA by choline acetyltransferase; rate-limiting step is choline availability.
Broken down by acetylcholinesterase to choline; no reuptake as such, but choline is re-uptaken and recycled.
Functions: arousal, learning, memory, REM sleep, pain, thirst, parasympathetic mediation.
Muscarinic receptors: G-protein coupled, M1-M5; nicotinic: ion channels, mediate attention in CNS.
Reduced cholinergic function in Alzheimer's dementia; dopamine balance affected in Parkinson's.

blocks.title: GABA at a glance
rows: Into presynaptic terminals and surrounding glia; bidirectional, temperature- and ion-dependent; inhibited by **tiagabine**
Mediates anxiety, seizure cessation, and actions of benzodiazepines, barbiturates and alcohol
Role in anxiety disorders and alcoholism; may be involved in epilepsy and Huntington's

blocks.title: GABA receptors
rows: Opens chloride channel; inhibitory, causing hyperpolarization; five subunits, at least 14 subunit subtypes
G-protein coupled; baclofen is the selective agonist

items.text: **GABA** is produced from glutamate (glutamic acid) by glutamic acid decarboxylase; glutamate is the precursor of **GABA**.
The enzyme that catabolises **GABA** is **GABA** transaminase (transaminase), alongside presynaptic reuptake.
Huntington's disease: disrupted GABAergic circuits - **GABA** was the keyed neurotransmitter.

bullets.text: GABA is synthesised from glutamate by glutamic acid decarboxylase (rate-limiting).
Broken down by GABA transaminase to glutamate, then succinic acid; reuptake into neurons and glia, inhibited by tiagabine.
Mediates anxiety, seizure cessation and the actions of benzodiazepines, barbiturates and alcohol.
GABA-A: chloride channel, inhibitory (hyperpolarization), five subunits; GABA-B: G-protein coupled, baclofen agonist.
Role in anxiety disorders and alcoholism; possibly epilepsy and Huntington's.

blocks.title: Glutamate at a glance
rows: (1) 2-oxoglutarate + aspartate via aspartate aminotransferase; (2) glutamine via glutaminase; (3) 2-oxoglutarate via ornithine aminotransferase
Accumulation of precursors such as glutamine, or end-product inhibition
Largely glial uptake with conversion to glutamine

Metabolic intermediary (oxidation/malate shuttle, ammonia cycle); immediate precursor of all **CNS** **GABA**; **NMDA**: memory acquisition, developmental plasticity, epilepsy, ischaemic brain injury; **NMDA** receptor mediates long-term potentiation
Excitotoxic glutamate toxicity suspected in stroke/schizophrenia/seizures; **NMDA** antagonists (**PCP**, **ketamine**) can cause hallucinations

blocks.title: Glutamate receptors
rows: Group I (mGluR1, mGluR5) linked to phospholipase C
Binding sites for glutamate, glycine, phencyclidine (**PCP**), magnesium and zinc

items.text: **Ketamine** is an antagonist (not selective agonist) at the **NMDA** receptor, binding the **PCP** site within the calcium channel - the incorrect statement about excitatory amino acids.
Glutamate was the keyed fast-acting excitatory neurotransmitter (major **CNS** excitatory transmitter, sometimes called the 'master switch' of the brain).
Glycine and D-serine are co-agonists at **NMDA** receptors.

blocks.note: **Q23**: **NMDA** receptors are predominantly located on **GABA** interneurons (inhibitory interneurons are about ==20%== of cortical neurons); this is not stated in the notes.
**Q27**: glutamate is the major excitatory **CNS** neurotransmitter ('master switch'); the notes do not state this directly.

bullets.text: Glutamate is synthesised by glutaminase (and from 2-oxoglutarate routes); broken down to glutamine or alpha-ketoglutarate; reuptake is largely glial.
It is the immediate precursor of all CNS GABA and has a metabolic role (malate shuttle, ammonia cycle).
NMDA receptor: memory acquisition, plasticity, epilepsy, ischaemic injury; mediates long-term potentiation.
Metabotropic: 8 receptors in 3 groups (Group I mGluR1/5 via phospholipase C); ionotropic: NMDA and non-NMDA (kainate, AMPA).
NMDA has binding sites for glutamate, glycine, PCP, magnesium and zinc.
Excitotoxicity suspected in stroke, schizophrenia, seizures; NMDA antagonists (PCP, ketamine) cause hallucinations.

blocks.text: Glycine is the primary inhibitory neurotransmitter in the spinal cord and has the simplest structure of all amino acids.
It is synthesised mainly from serine by serine trans-hydroxymethylase and glycerate dehydrogenase, both rate-limiting steps.

blocks.title: Two glycine receptor sites
rows: Excitatory glycine site on the **NMDA** receptor (non-strychnine-sensitive glycine receptor)
Glycine acts as a 'mandatory adjunctive neurotransmitter' for glutamate receptors

blocks.text: Facilitating glycine transmission can help reduce negative symptoms of schizophrenia; bitopertin, an experimental glycine reuptake inhibitor, showed early promise.
Glycine and D-serine both act as co-agonists at **NMDA** receptors; the same explanation also notes glycine is an independent inhibitory neurotransmitter at its own receptors.

bullets.text: Primary inhibitory neurotransmitter in the spinal cord; simplest amino acid.
Synthesised from serine (serine trans-hydroxymethylase, glycerate dehydrogenase - both rate-limiting).
Mandatory adjunctive transmitter at the NMDA receptor (non-strychnine-sensitive site); strychnine-sensitive receptor is inhibitory in the spinal cord.
Facilitating glycine transmission may reduce negative symptoms; bitopertin (glycine reuptake inhibitor) is experimental.

blocks.text: Both endocannabinoids are formed from arachidonic acid and ethanolamine.
There are two cannabinoid receptor types, central (**CB1**) and peripheral (**CB2**); both bind tetrahydrocannabinol (**THC**), the active ingredient of marijuana.
Anandamide lowers intraocular pressure, decreases activity level and relieves pain.

bullets.text: Two endocannabinoids: anandamide (weak ligand) and 2-arachidonylglycerol (strong ligand), formed from arachidonic acid and ethanolamine.
CB1 central, CB2 peripheral; both bind THC.
Anandamide lowers intraocular pressure, reduces activity and relieves pain.

blocks.text: Neurotrophins are polypeptide growth factors influencing proliferation and differentiation of neurons and glial cells. Best characterised: nerve growth factor (**NGF**), brain derived neurotrophic factor (**BDNF**), neurotrophin 3 and neurotrophin 4.

Neurotrophin hypothesis: neurons compete during development for the limited growth factors in the target region; highly responsive neurons (e.g. high-affinity binding sites) survive while others undergo programmed cell death. Incorrect axon targeting may also cause apoptosis.
**BDNF** may have a role in long-term potentiation (**LTP**) of memory. In animals, chronic stress down-regulates **BDNF**; **BDNF** has trophic effects on serotonergic and noradrenergic neurons.
SSRIs and other antidepressants including **ECT** up-regulate **BDNF**, and the time course of this up-regulation coincides with the therapeutic actions of antidepressant interventions.

blocks.title: BDNF Val66Met polymorphism
rows: Single nucleotide polymorphism in **BDNF** gene on chromosome 11p13: valine -> methionine at codon 66 (Val66Met)
Val66Met allele carriers: impaired hippocampal activation and performance
Controversial whether the polymorphism increases risk of clinical disorders

bullets.text: Neurotrophins are polypeptide growth factors: NGF, BDNF, neurotrophin 3 and 4.
Neurotrophin hypothesis: neurons compete for limited growth factor; poor responders undergo programmed cell death.
BDNF: role in LTP of memory; down-regulated by chronic stress (animals); trophic to serotonergic and noradrenergic neurons.
SSRIs, other antidepressants and ECT up-regulate BDNF, with a time course matching therapeutic response.
Val66Met (11p13, codon 66) reduces BDNF activity; met/met mice more anxious; human carriers have impaired hippocampal activation; disease risk controversial.

blocks.title: Clinical implications of neurochemistry
rows: Chronic antidepressant treatment reduces beta adrenoceptor density about 2 weeks after starting, correlating with therapeutic effect; unmedicated suicide victims show higher beta adrenoceptor density; beta blockade can reduce peripheral features of anxiety driven by sympathetic overdrive

Post-mortem studies of depressed/suicidal patients show increased 5HT2 binding sites (increase in 5HT2A most prominent in dorsolateral prefrontal cortex and in platelets of medication-naive patients) and reduced 5HT1A receptors in cortex

Long-term antidepressants reduce 5HT2 receptors and increase 5HT1A function, but these changes may not cause the antidepressant action since they predate clinical response; most directly acting 5HT1A agonists have poor antidepressant activity

Brain ACh reduced in **DLB**, similar to Alzheimer's; cortical ChAT reduced more (==85%==) in **DLB** patients with hallucinations than those without (==50%==); may partly explain altered sleep-wake patterns and response of hallucinations to acetylcholinesterase inhibitors

blocks.text: Aberrant salience (Kapur, 2003): in the normal individual mesolimbic dopamine attaches significance (salience) to an external stimulus or internal thought, turning neutral information into attention-grabbing information.

In acute psychosis the hyperdopaminergic mesolimbic state gives insignificant events and perceptions inappropriate salience, leading to delusional elaborations. Antipsychotics are claimed to 'dampen the salience' of these experiences - they do not erase symptoms but provide the platform for psychological resolution.

bullets.text: Beta adrenoceptor density falls ~2 weeks into antidepressant treatment, correlating with response; higher in unmedicated suicide victims.
Beta blockade reduces peripheral features of sympathetically driven anxiety.
Depressed/suicidal patients: raised 5HT2 binding (5HT2A, DLPFC and platelets) and reduced cortical 5HT1A.
Long-term antidepressants reduce 5HT2 and increase 5HT1A function, but this predates clinical response; direct 5HT1A agonists are poor antidepressants.
DLB: reduced ACh; cortical ChAT down 85% with hallucinations vs 50% without; hallucinations respond to acetylcholinesterase inhibitors.
Aberrant salience (Kapur): hyperdopaminergic mesolimbic state gives inappropriate salience -> delusions; antipsychotics dampen salience.

facts.label: ChAT reduction in DLB with hallucinations
ChAT reduction in DLB without hallucinations
